note: Proverbs 27:17's epigraph quotes only Segond's first half (« Comme le fer aiguise le fer… »): Segond's second half (« Ainsi un homme excite la colère d’un homme ») means the opposite of the KJV's “sharpeneth the countenance of his friend”, which the chapter builds on.

Every epigraph replaces the English KJV verse with the whole verse verbatim from Louis Segond (1910), dropping the “(KJV)” label; the only changes are French spacing before : ; ? ! and, in 1 Peter 3:15 (ch9), Segond's trailing comma dropped, and in Ecclesiastes 3:4 (ch12) the initial « un » capitalised. Ecclesiastes 5:4 (English numbering) is Ecclésiaste 5:3 in Segond and is cited as such.

Proverbs 27:17 in Segond reads « Ainsi un homme excite la colère d’un homme » — a different sense from the KJV's “sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” that the chapter builds on; the whole Segond verse is kept as the epigraph and the body only reuses the shared first half (« le fer aiguise le fer »). A native reviewer may prefer a partial epigraph.

Lewis's own words (“the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England”, the Whipsnade sentence, the first line of A Grief Observed) are plain renderings of our own, not taken from any published French translation; the convert line matches the children's French edition. King Lear's “Men must endure their going hence” is rendered « Les hommes doivent endurer leur départ d’ici-bas » (also the ch13 title stem).

Names and titles follow c-s-lewis-a-life-children.fr: Mme Moore, le Grand Coup, les Kilns, collège de Magdalen, église de la Sainte-Trinité, père Adams, Le Monde de Narnia, Tactique du diable, Les Fondements du christianisme, Apprendre la mort, Le Seigneur des anneaux; also Le Problème de la souffrance, L’Homme éternel (Chesterton), Le Roi Lear, and Shadowlands as « Les Ombres du cœur (Shadowlands) ». Eight acres became « plus de trois hectares »; narration is in the passé simple and the reader is addressed with « tu », as in a-retrospect-teens.fr.
